paragraphs: Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Chullin 107a): one may wash the hands only from a vessel, because they based the law of the purity of the hands on the sprinkling of the water of purification (mei chatat) and on the sanctification of the hands and feet in the Temple, which required a vessel — for regarding the sanctification of hands and feet it is stated (Exodus 30:18-19), "You shall make a laver, etc., and they shall wash from it, etc.", and regarding the water of purification it is stated (Numbers 19:17), "and one shall put upon it living water, into a vessel." And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Chullin 107a): all vessels are valid, even vessels of stone and vessels of earth, which are not considered vessels with respect to the laws of impurity — nevertheless they are valid here, provided they are made to hold liquid. But felt caps — even if hard, and even if made of leather that can hold liquid — are invalid for the washing of the hands, since they are not complete vessels for use, and also since they were not made to hold liquid. In a time of pressing need, when one has no other vessel and cannot find one, Maran, of blessed memory, permitted washing with them, but one should not recite the blessing over the washing of the hands; and it is good that one wrap his hands in a cloth after washing with such vessels, and eat while his hands remain wrapped in the cloth — see Mishbetzot Zahav and the other later authorities, of blessed memory.

clarification.explanation: Our sages established that washing the hands must be done specifically from a vessel (and not, for example, directly from a tap or a river without a vessel), because they compared the law of the purity of the hands to the law of sprinkling the water of purification and to the sanctification of the hands and feet of the priests in the Temple — where it is explicitly stated that a vessel was required ("You shall make a laver... and they shall wash from it", "and he shall put upon it living water into a vessel"). All types of vessels are valid for washing, including vessels of stone and of earth, which for the laws of impurity are not considered vessels — here they are valid, provided they are made to hold liquid. But felt caps (thick cloth material) — even if hard and even if made of leather that can hold liquid — are invalid for washing, since they are not considered "complete vessels" for use, and were also not originally made to hold liquid. In a time of pressing need, when there is no other vessel, Maran permitted washing with such a cap, but without reciting the blessing over the washing of the hands, and it is good to wrap the hands afterward in a cloth and eat that way.
takeaways: Washing the hands must be done from a vessel (any vessel, including stone and earthenware, if made to hold liquid).
Objects that are not a "complete vessel" made to hold liquid (such as a cloth cap) are invalid; in great pressing need, one may use them without a blessing.

paragraphs: Also the covers of vessels — since they were not originally made to hold [liquid] — one may not wash from them; see the Shulchan Aruch of Rabbeinu Zalman, section 6, and Chayei Adam and the other later authorities.

clarification.explanation: The covers of vessels (lids) are also invalid for washing the hands, since from the outset they were not made to hold liquid (but only to cover), and therefore they do not have the law of a "vessel" with regard to washing.
takeaways: A vessel's cover is not valid for washing the hands, since it was not originally made to hold liquid.

paragraphs: The vessel must hold a revi'it; and if it does not hold a revi'it, one may not wash the hands from it, even if one fills it two or three times, pouring from it onto the hands several revi'iyot [in total].

clarification.explanation: The vessel from which one washes must hold at least the measure of a "revi'it" (roughly a quarter of a log, a specific liquid measure) all at once. If the vessel does not hold a revi'it, one may not wash from it — even if it is filled several times and the total amount poured onto the hands equals several revi'iyot — because each time, the vessel itself must contain a full revi'it measure at the moment of pouring.
takeaways: The vessel must hold a full revi'it all at once; it does not help to fill a small vessel several times and accumulate a revi'it's worth cumulatively.

paragraphs: The vessel must not be perforated. There are two kinds of holes: one is called "letting liquid out," and the second is called "letting liquid in" — that is, if one places this vessel into water, the water enters it through that hole, and this hole is larger than a hole that only lets liquid out. Now, if the hole is of the "letting liquid in" kind, then even if the vessel holds a revi'it from the hole downward, one may not wash from it, since once it has such a hole it is entirely voided from the law of a vessel. But if the hole is small, only of the "letting liquid out" kind, then if [the part] from the hole downward holds a revi'it, one may wash from it, and if not, one may not wash from it. However, if one has another vessel, even though this one holds a revi'it from the hole downward, one should not wash from it ab initio.

clarification.explanation: The vessel used for washing must not be perforated. There are two kinds of holes: a "letting-out" hole — a small hole through which liquid seeps out of the vessel; and a "letting-in" hole — a larger hole, such that if the vessel is submerged in water, the water enters it through the hole. If the hole is of the "letting-in" kind, the entire vessel is invalid for washing, even if a revi'it's worth still remains below the level of the hole, since a hole of this kind entirely voids the vessel from the law of a "vessel." If the hole is only of the "letting-out" kind (smaller), the vessel is valid, provided the portion below the hole holds a revi'it; if not, it is invalid. But even when the vessel is valid (with a small hole and a revi'it below it), if the person has another sound vessel, it is preferable that he not use the perforated vessel in the first place.
takeaways: A hole of the "letting-in" kind (large) invalidates the vessel entirely, even if a revi'it's worth remains in it.
A hole of the "letting-out" kind (small) is valid after the fact if a revi'it remains below the hole, but it is preferable to avoid it and use a sound vessel if available.

paragraphs: Some say that the distinction between "letting liquid in" and "letting liquid out" applies only to a hole; but if the vessel has cracked, then even though it is only [of the severity of] "letting liquid out," one may not wash from it, because a crack is worse than a hole. And even though there are those who disagree and hold that no distinction should be made, one should be concerned for the opinion of those who are stringent, and only in a time of pressing need may one rely on those who are lenient — but one should not recite the blessing with [God's] Name and Kingship, but rather should contemplate the Name and Kingship in his heart. See Chayei Adam and the other later authorities.

clarification.explanation: Some hold that the distinction between "letting liquid in" (a large hole, which invalidates) and "letting liquid out" (a small hole, valid with a revi'it) applies only where there is an actual hole. But a vessel that has cracked — even if the crack is small, only at the level of "letting liquid out" — is entirely invalid, because a crack is more severe than a hole. There are those who disagree, but one should be concerned for the stringent opinion; only in a time of pressing need may one rely on the lenient view, and in such a case one should not recite the blessing with [God's] Name and Kingship ("Blessed are You, Lord...") but should say it without the Name and Kingship, contemplating them in his heart instead.
takeaways: A cracked vessel (even a small crack) is more severe than a perforated one — it is invalid even where a hole of the same size would have been valid.
In a time of pressing need one may be lenient, but should recite the blessing without [God's] Name and Kingship, contemplating them in the heart instead.

paragraphs: Any hole or crack from which water comes out drop after drop, in close succession, one after another — this is certainly known to be the measure of "letting liquid in," and it is invalid according to all opinions. But if it does not release drop after drop, then one should test it by placing it in water and seeing whether it lets liquid in or not.

clarification.explanation: The way to test the type of hole: a hole or crack from which drops of water emerge one after another in close succession is certainly known to be of the "letting liquid in" measure — the severe kind — and is invalid according to all opinions. If the hole does not drip in this way, one should test it by submerging the vessel in water and observing whether water penetrates inward through it (letting liquid in) or not.
takeaways: A steady drip of drops from a hole indicates "letting liquid in" (invalid according to all opinions); otherwise, one should test by submerging the vessel in water.

paragraphs: A vessel called in Arabic "ibriq" (a jug/pitcher with a spout) — the common practice in the Land of Israel and in Turkey is to wash from it, as the Gaon Chida, of blessed memory, wrote in Machazik Berachah, and this is also the common practice here in our city of Baghdad, may it be protected. However, some are stringent and say that if the mouth of the spout is higher than the mouth of the wide opening, one should wash through the wide opening, and it is good to be careful about this where possible — see Chesed LaAlafim, letter 2, and the other later authorities, of blessed memory. And know that all copper ibriq vessels commonly found here in our city, may it be protected, typically have a higher spout. There is also another distinction: in earthenware vessels, the mouths are straight and round, without a protruding spout-like lip made for pouring, but in copper vessels, a protruding, spout-like lip is made at the tip of the narrow spout, from which one pours. Regarding this there is another concern, namely that some prohibit washing through that spout-shaped part, because it does not have the law of a "vessel," since it does not hold liquids there, and according to them one must wash through the wide [straight] opening, which is not made in the shape of a spout. Although there are those who disagree and hold that it is permitted to wash through there as well — see on this Rav Matteh Yehudah and the other later authorities, and so the Gaon Machazik Berachah testified that this is the common practice, as mentioned above — nevertheless, one who fears Heaven should be concerned about this and should not wash through there, but should wash through the wide mouth, which is the straight place that holds liquids. However, one should not protest against those who follow the lenient practice of washing through the spout. In any case, you see that this earthenware ibriq commonly found here in our city, which stands straight both at the spout and at the wide opening, is preferable for washing from, and one should wash from the mouth of the narrow spout, which is lower than the mouth of the wide opening.

clarification.explanation: A vessel called an "ibriq" (a jug/pitcher with a pouring spout) — the prevalent custom in the Land of Israel and in Turkey, and likewise in Baghdad, is to wash the hands from it as usual. Some are stringent and say that if the mouth of the spout is higher than the mouth of the wide opening, one should wash specifically through the wide opening, and it is good to be careful about this when possible (in Baghdad, the local copper vessels tend to have a higher spout). There is a further difference: in earthenware vessels, the spout's mouth is round and straight without a protrusion, but in copper vessels a spout-shaped protrusion is made at the tip for convenient pouring — and some invalidate washing through that spout, since it is so narrow that it is not considered a "vessel" that holds liquid, and in their view one should wash only through the wide opening. Others disagree and permit washing through the spout as well, and so the Chida testified that this is the prevalent practice. Nevertheless, one who fears Heaven should be careful and avoid washing through the spout, though one should not protest against those who follow the lenient practice. The earthenware ibriq common in Baghdad, whose mouth is straight and not spout-shaped, is preferable — and one should wash specifically through the mouth of the narrow spout, which is lower than the wide mouth, so there is no such concern.
takeaways: An ibriq (pitcher) is valid for washing. In a copper vessel whose spout is high and shaped like a protruding spout, one who fears Heaven should prefer to wash through the wide mouth; but in the earthenware vessel, whose spout is lower than the wide mouth, one should wash specifically through the spout.

paragraphs: One must be careful that the rim of the vessel from which one washes does not have a groove or protrusion of the measure of "letting liquid in." And if the vessel's rim is broken on one side, one should wash at the place of the break, which is the lower and lowest part.

clarification.explanation: One must be careful that the rim of the vessel used for washing does not have a groove or protrusion at the severe measure of "letting liquid in" (which could cause the vessel to be considered defective). If the vessel's rim is broken on one side, one should wash specifically at the place of the break, which is the lower part.
takeaways: One should check that the vessel's rim does not have a severe groove or protrusion; a vessel broken at its rim — one should wash through the place of the break (the lower point).

paragraphs: A perforated copper vessel is not helped by sealing it with wax, nor with clay, nor with pitch, nor with the glue called in Arabic "gigi," nor with what is called "qir" (pitch/tar), nor with anything similar to these — rather, it must be sealed with tin, and that will help it. And any earthenware vessel is not helped by sealing with potter's clay or mud, but is helped by pitch and glue. See Sedeh Ha'aretz, section 3. Therefore, here in our city, one must be careful when purchasing an earthenware ibriq to see whether it has been repaired with potter's clay, because here in our city new holes are found, and the seller notices them and repairs them with the potter's clay called in Arabic "tzala'ch" (porcelain-clay), and this is quite common; therefore the buyer should pay careful attention to examine the vessel, lest it has been repaired in this manner, and should not purchase such a vessel for the purpose of washing the hands.

clarification.explanation: A perforated copper vessel is not helped by sealing with wax, mud, pitch ("qir"), or glue ("gigi") and the like — only sealing with tin is effective and restores the vessel's validity. By contrast, an earthenware vessel is not helped by sealing with potter's clay or mud, but pitch and glue are effective for it. In Baghdad, one must be careful when purchasing an earthenware ibriq to check whether it has been improperly "repaired" with potter's clay — since sellers commonly patch new holes that form in a vessel with potter's clay ("tzala'ch"), and such a repair is not effective; therefore the buyer must examine the vessel carefully so as not to purchase such a vessel for the purpose of washing the hands.
takeaways: A perforated copper vessel: only sealing with tin is effective. An earthenware vessel: only pitch/glue are effective, not potter's clay.
One should check when purchasing that an earthenware ibriq was not repaired with potter's clay, which is not effective.

paragraphs: One should not fill his cupped hands with water and give them to his friend to pour onto his hands, since one may wash only from a vessel. Likewise, a person himself should not wash one hand from the vessel and then pour from it onto his other hand. Some permit this in a case where he poured a full revi'it at once from the vessel onto the first hand, since that first hand [having received a full revi'it directly] from the vessel, it is then effective if he pours from it onto the second hand — nevertheless, one should be stringent in accordance with the first opinion, which invalidates this in every case.

clarification.explanation: One may not fill his cupped hands with water and give them to a friend for washing, since washing must be done specifically from a vessel and not from a cupped hand. Likewise, a person himself may not wash one hand from the vessel and then pour from it onto his other hand (since the hand that was washed is not considered a "vessel"). Some permit this only when a full revi'it was poured onto the first hand all at once from the vessel — since then the first hand itself has the law of "washed from a vessel" sufficiently — but nevertheless one should be stringent in accordance with the first opinion, which invalidates this in every case.
takeaways: One may not wash hands from another person's cupped hand, and may not pour water with which one hand was already washed onto the other hand — one should be stringent about this.

paragraphs: If one placed his hands into a vessel of water and rubbed his hands together in it, this does not constitute valid washing if the vessel is attached to the ground, since, the vessel being attached to the ground, there is no washing here at all, but rather this is like an immersion, and there is no [valid] immersion in drawn water. But if the vessel is not attached to the ground, this is a manner of washing, and some permit it, holding that whether one washes his hands by pouring from the vessel or by inserting his hands into the vessel, all of this is called "washing from a vessel," while others forbid it. In a time of pressing need, when one has no vessel to pour from, one may rely on those who are lenient, but should recite the blessing without [God's] Name and Kingship, contemplating the Name and Kingship in his heart instead, and should also wrap his hands in a cloth before eating.

clarification.explanation: If one inserted his hands into a vessel of water and rubbed them together inside, without pouring — if the vessel is attached to the ground (such as an attached pit), this is not considered valid washing at all, but rather a kind of immersion, and drawn water is invalid for immersion (since immersion requires a natural mikveh, not water that was drawn into it). But if the vessel is not attached to the ground (an ordinary portable vessel), some hold that even inserting the hands into it and rubbing them there is considered valid washing (whether one washes by pouring from the vessel or by inserting the hands into it), while others forbid this. In a time of pressing need, when there is no other vessel to pour from, one may rely on the lenient opinion, but should recite the blessing without [God's] Name and Kingship (contemplation only), and it is also proper to wrap the hands afterward in a cloth before eating.
takeaways: Inserting the hands into a vessel attached to the ground and rubbing them there is not considered valid washing at all.
In a portable vessel — there is a dispute, and in pressing need one may be lenient without reciting the blessing aloud.

paragraphs: One who has no vessel may immerse his hands in a river, or in a mikveh that contains forty se'ah valid for the immersion of women, or in a spring even though it does not contain forty se'ah, provided only that his hands become covered by the water all at once, and he should recite the blessing over the washing of the hands. And even though strictly speaking it suffices to immerse the hands once, and no drying is even required, nevertheless in this case as well one should immerse three times and rub [the hands] three times, because there is a mystical secret in the matter; and the drying will in any case be done for the sake of cleanliness.

And this permission to immerse the hands in a river applies specifically to the great rivers that come and flow of themselves from the mountains, such as the Tigris and the Euphrates, and the Amanah and the Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, and the like. But those rivers which are [really] channels dug by the owners of fields, made in fields and vineyards in order to irrigate the trees and crops, into which water is drawn from the great river or from the spring by means of a bucket that is poured into a pool, and from the pool the water is drawn onward into these channels, which are the small rivers — it is forbidden to immerse the hands in these, for even though they contain forty se'ah or more, because they are very long, even though they are not deep, and moreover they are drawn water that has been conveyed [into them] — since the bucket pours into the pool and from the pool the water is drawn onward to the river — nevertheless they are considered flowing (zochalin) and are invalid; and wherever no barrier has been made within them to stop the flow of the water so that it collects and stands still rather than flowing, one may not immerse the hands in them. And if one immerses his hands in that pool into which the bucket pours, immersing while the bucket is still pouring — even though some permit this on the grounds that a poured stream (nitzok) constitutes a connection, since the bucket is perforated and, while it pours into the pool, it is in effect pouring into the spring as well — nevertheless, since there are those who hold that a poured stream is not a connection, one should not rely on leniency in this matter. However, sometimes within these channels that pass through fields and vineyards, people construct one large and deep pool that contains forty se'ah of water collected within it; in such a pool it is permitted to immerse the hands, since the water is collected within it. But one must be careful to insert his hands into the pool below the level of the bottom of the channel that pours the water into the pool and out of it, because the upper surface of the pool, level with the water passing over the channel, is considered there to be flowing; therefore one must lower his hands down into the water that is collected within the pool, and the measure of forty se'ah likewise must be present in the collected water, not measured from the top of the pool.

clarification.explanation:
One who has no vessel may immerse his hands in a river or in a mikveh containing forty se'ah valid for women's immersion, or in a spring even though it does not contain forty se'ah, provided his hands become covered by the water all at once, and he recites the blessing "al netilat yadayim." And although strictly it suffices to immerse once, with no need for drying, nevertheless one should immerse three times and rub three times, because there is a secret in this matter; the drying will be done anyway for cleanliness.
The permission to immerse the hands in a river applies specifically to the great rivers that come and flow of themselves from the mountains (such as the Tigris, the Euphrates, and the rivers of Damascus and the like). But channels dug by the owners of fields and vineyards to irrigate their trees and crops, drawing water from the river or spring by bucket into a pool and from there onward into the channels — it is forbidden to immerse the hands in these, even though they contain forty se'ah, because they are "drawn water" and "flowing" (zochalin) — and invalid — unless a barrier was made in them to stop the flow of the water so that it collects and stands still. And even if one immerses in the pool while the bucket is still pouring into it — although some permit this on the grounds of "a poured stream is a connection" — since there are those who hold "a poured stream is not a connection," one should not rely on leniency here. However, if within these channels a large, deep pool was built that contains forty se'ah of collected water, it is permitted to immerse the hands in it; but one must be careful to insert the hands below the level of the bottom of the inflow/outflow channel (since the upper surface, level with the water passing through the channel, is considered "flowing"), and should lower the hands into the collected water; and the measure of forty se'ah must likewise be present in the collected water itself, not measured from the top of the pool.
takeaways: One with no vessel immerses his hands in a large river / a mikveh of forty se'ah / a spring (so that they are covered all at once) and recites the blessing; and immerses and rubs three times (a mystical reason).
A natural river flowing from the mountains is valid; irrigation channels (drawn and flowing water) are invalid unless the water is collected and standing still.
In a deep pool containing forty se'ah of collected water, it is permitted, but one must lower the hands below the level of the channel, into the collected water.

paragraphs: If one washed one hand and immersed [only] one hand, it is valid, and he recites the blessing "al netilat yadayim" [in the plural] according to all opinions. Likewise, if one hand has a wound upon which water cannot be placed and it is wrapped in cloth, and he washes only the other hand, he should recite the blessing "al netilat yadayim" and should not recite "al netilat yad" [in the singular], as I have written in a responsum in my small book, Rav Pe'alim.

clarification.explanation: If one washed only one hand (for example, immersing only that hand), the washing is valid, and one recites "al netilat yadayim" (in the plural) even according to all opinions. Likewise, one who has a wound on one hand upon which water cannot be placed, and it is wrapped in cloth, and who washes only the other hand — he too recites "al netilat yadayim" (in the usual plural form), and not "al netilat yad" (singular).
takeaways: Even when only one hand is washed (due to a wound on the other), one recites "al netilat yadayim" in the ordinary [plural] wording, not the singular.

paragraphs: The water must come onto the hands by the force of a person ("ko'ach gavra"), and if it came of itself, this is not considered valid washing. Therefore, a vessel called in Arabic "manzabla" (a water container with a faucet) that has a spigot shaped like a copper rooster's head, which one turns to one side and the water comes out — one who washes his hands from it must open and close it several times in close succession, for if this is not done, only the first spurt is considered to come by the force of a person, and this first spurt does not contain enough water to cover the entire hand.

clarification.explanation: The water must reach the hands through a direct human action ("by the force of a person"), and if the water reached the hands of itself (for example, from an open tap that continues flowing on its own), this is not valid washing. Therefore, with a vessel called "manzabla" (a water container with a faucet shaped like a rooster's head), the one washing must open and close the faucet several times in succession during the washing — for if he does not do so, only the first stream (at the moment of opening) is considered to come by the force of the person, and this initial stream usually does not contain enough water to cover the whole hand.
takeaways: The water must reach the hands "by the force of a person" and not of itself — with a faucet, one must open and close it several times in succession to ensure that a sufficient amount comes by the force of the opening itself.

paragraphs: One should not have his hands washed [poured for him] by a minor who has not completed six full years, because washing the hands requires intention, and such a minor's law is like that of a monkey, which has no understanding, as mentioned in the later authorities. And it is good to be careful not to have one's hands washed by a gentile, and likewise not by one's sister or daughter who are in a state of niddah, or by another woman, even if she is not a niddah — one should also not [have water poured by them]. But if the gentile or the niddah brought the water in a vessel and he himself pours it and washes, this is permitted. And one who is careful about this as well, blessing will come upon him, as mentioned in the later authorities.

clarification.explanation: One should not have his hands washed by a minor under six full years of age, since washing the hands requires intention, and such a minor is considered as lacking sufficient understanding ("like a monkey"). It is also good to be careful not to have one's hands washed by a gentile, nor by a sister or daughter who are in a state of niddah (ritual impurity of menstruation), nor by any other woman even if she is not a niddah. But if the gentile or the woman merely brought the water in a vessel, and the person himself pours and washes his own hands (only taking the vessel from them), this is permitted. One who is careful about this as well (not accepting water directly from women at all) is deserving of blessing.
takeaways: One should not have his hands washed by a child under six years of age, and it is recommended not to receive water directly from a gentile, a niddah, or a woman — but it is permitted if they merely bring the vessel and the person himself does the washing.

paragraphs: There are seven liquids that receive impurity "without [prior] preparation": the first is wine, and vinegar is included in this; the second is bees' honey after it has been separated from the wax, as mentioned in Matteh Yosef, part 2, page 9, column 3; the third is olive oil; the fourth is [animal] fat, and milk-water is included in this; the fifth is dew; the sixth is the blood of cattle, wild animals, and fowl; and the seventh is water — and their mnemonic is "YAD SHACHAT DAM" (an acronym). But other fruit juices, even if made into beverages for drinking, do not receive impurity "without preparation." Therefore, one who eats something whose "dipping" (tibul) was in a liquid from among the liquids mentioned, or upon which one of them was spilled while it is still moist — even though the food does not touch the place of the liquid, and even if one eats it with a spoon — must wash his hands first, but should not recite the blessing over the washing of the hands, since our Rabbis instituted the blessing only specifically for one who washes his hands to eat bread. And even though blood is forbidden to eat for its own separate reason, it was counted among the seven liquids on account of a person who eats it for medicinal purposes or in a life-threatening situation. However, fish blood is not called a "liquid" for this purpose, and therefore one who eats fish with its blood does not require washing of the hands.

clarification.explanation: There are seven kinds of liquids that receive impurity "without preparation" (that is, they receive impurity from mere contact, without any special preparatory act): wine (vinegar included), bees' honey (once separated from the wax), olive oil, milk (milk-water included), dew, the blood of cattle/wild animals/fowl, and water — the mnemonic is "YAD SHACHAT DAM" (an acronym of wine, honey, oil, milk, dew, blood, water). Other fruit juices, even if made for drinking, do not receive impurity without preparation. From this the halachah follows: one who eats something that was "dipped" in one of these seven liquids, or upon which one of them was spilled while still moist (even if it does not touch the place of the liquid itself), and even if one eats with a spoon — must wash his hands first, but should not recite the blessing over this washing (since our Rabbis instituted the blessing only for washing before eating bread). Blood, although forbidden to eat in its own right, is included among the seven liquids because sometimes it is eaten for medicinal purposes or in a case of danger to life. Fish blood is not considered a "liquid" for this purpose, so one who eats fish with its blood is not obligated in washing the hands.
takeaways: The seven liquids that convey impurity without preparation: wine, (bees') honey, olive oil, milk, dew, blood (of cattle/wild animals/fowl), and water.
One who eats something dipped in one of them must wash the hands without a blessing — except for fish blood, which is not considered a liquid for this purpose.

paragraphs: Even one who eats less than a kezayit (an olive's volume) of things whose dipping was in a liquid from among the liquids mentioned must wash his hands, and the proof for this is from the night of Pesach, when one eats karpas in an amount less than a kezayit, and nevertheless one is obligated to wash the hands because of its dipping in a liquid, as mentioned in Birkei Yosef.

clarification.explanation: Even one who eats less than a kezayit (a minimal measure of eating) of something whose dipping was in one of the seven liquids that convey impurity must wash his hands. The proof for this is from the Seder night, when one eats karpas (dipped in salt water or vinegar) in an amount less than a kezayit, and nevertheless is obligated to wash the hands beforehand on account of its dipping in a liquid — not on account of the measure of eating.
takeaways: The obligation to wash the hands due to dipping in a liquid applies even to eating less than a kezayit — as is the practice regarding the karpas on the Seder night.

paragraphs: Any of the liquids mentioned that was cooked together with other things, and there remains in them, of the liquids mentioned, [a quantity of] "tofei'ach al menat lehatpiach" (moist enough to further moisten something else), one must wash the hands before eating them. Likewise, if something was soaked in water, or fruits were washed in water and remain wet such that there is upon them water of the measure "tofei'ach al menat lehatpiach," one must wash the hands. Some are lenient regarding a cooked item, permitting one to eat it with a spoon without washing, and one may rely on the lenient opinion where there is pressing need and great difficulty. However, regarding preserves (jam) given to a guest by means of a fork, one may permit this readily, since this is considered something that is customarily eaten with a spoon [utensil], for it would be disgraceful to take a piece of the preserve by hand to eat it without a fork — and the proof is that if they had no fork, they would not serve the preserve without one. However, all this applies only to a preserve in which water predominates, or is half and half; but where the sugar and fruit are more than the water in which they were cooked, no washing is required at all. See Matteh Yosef, part 2, page 9, column 2, and the other later authorities.

clarification.explanation: When a liquid among the seven that convey impurity was cooked together with other things, and the resulting mixture itself retains moisture of the measure "tofei'ach al menat lehatpiach" (wet enough to moisten something else in turn), one must wash the hands before eating it. Likewise, if something was soaked in water, or fruit was washed in water and remains wet to this same degree, washing is required. Some are lenient regarding eating a cooked item by means of a spoon (without direct hand contact) without washing, and one may rely on this leniency in a case of pressing need and great difficulty. But preserves (jam) served to a guest by means of a fork may be permitted readily, since this is considered something customarily eaten with a utensil (a fork), not directly by hand (the proof being that if there were no fork, the preserve would not be served without one at all). However, this leniency applies only to a preserve in which water predominates or is equal to the fruit; where the sugar and fruit exceed the water in which they were cooked, no washing is required at all.
takeaways: A cooked food with moisture of the "tofei'ach al menat lehatpiach" measure requires washing, but one may be lenient if eating it with a spoon in a case of pressing difficulty.
Preserves in which water predominates, eaten with a fork, are permitted without washing; if sugar/fruit predominate (little water), no washing is required at all.

paragraphs: A liquid among those mentioned that has been cooked — one may dip bread into it and eat without washing the hands, because the liquid is cooked and also because one's hands do not touch the place that was dipped. Therefore one must be careful in this matter, that one's hands not touch the place where the food is dipped in the liquid, as Rav Neveh Shalom wrote, page 135. And what the Gaon Chida, of blessed memory, demonstrated concerning those who dip bread in "kahveh" [coffee] and eat without washing the hands — this is because they do not touch it with their hands. And one who drinks from these liquids mentioned, from a vessel, does not require washing of the hands; but one who dips his finger [in the liquid] and sucks it, and likewise one who drinks water from his cupped hands, requires washing of the hands. Some are lenient regarding one who dips his finger and drinks with his hand, holding that our Rabbis instituted washing for liquids only by way of dipping foods, and not in any other manner; and although one who is lenient has a basis to rely upon, nevertheless one should be careful where possible.

clarification.explanation: A liquid among the seven that has been cooked — one may dip bread in it and eat without washing the hands, since the liquid is cooked and also because the hands do not touch the place of dipping. One must be careful not to touch the place of dipping with the hands. The reason those who dip bread in cooked "coffee" (kahveh) and eat without washing were permitted to do so is only when they do not touch it with their hands — not when they do touch it. One who drinks one of the seven liquids from a vessel (by drinking directly) does not require washing of the hands at all; but one who dips a finger into the liquid and sucks it, and likewise one who drinks water from his cupped hands, requires washing of the hands. Some are lenient regarding one who dips a finger and drinks from his hand, holding that our Rabbis instituted washing for liquids only in the case of dipping food, and not in any other manner. Although the lenient position has a basis to rely upon, one should nevertheless be careful where possible.
takeaways: Dipping bread in a cooked liquid without touching the dipped place with the hands is permitted without washing.
Drinking from a vessel requires no washing; dipping a finger and sucking it, or drinking from cupped hands, requires washing (some are lenient, but it is proper to be careful).

paragraphs: Butter, if it is congealed, is not a liquid but is considered a food; but if it has melted, it is a liquid and requires washing of the hands. And distilled liquor ("burnt wine") made from grain or from dates and the like is not considered a liquid for this purpose, since it is only [considered] vapor/sweat. As for roasted meat upon which its own juice drips — some say it requires washing of the hands, and some say it does not require it, and one may rely on those who permit it.

clarification.explanation: Butter: if it is congealed, it is food (no washing required); but if it has melted, it is a liquid, and washing is required. "Burnt wine" (a distilled spirit) made from grain or dates and the like is not considered a liquid for this purpose, since it is only [considered like] vapor. And roasted meat upon which its own drippings are moist — some say washing of the hands is required, and some say it is not required, and one may rely on those who are lenient that washing is not required.
takeaways: Congealed butter is food (no washing); melted butter is a liquid (washing required). "Burnt wine" is not considered a liquid for this purpose.
Roasted meat with dripping juice — disputed; one may rely on the lenient view that washing is not required.
